response.text:
One thing I often hear from people is how their inner child doesn’t trust them, usually despite the fact that the person has just said 3 nice things to him/her in meditation.

To this I respond with a few things. First of all, we have three ‘adults’ (that is aspects of the present day person) to do reparenting: the Nurturer, the Protector and the Leader/Guru. It’s important to keep in mind that these ‘adults’ are not separate people inside you, but merely the different functions of the present day person that are used for reparenting.

Secondly, the inner child also has something to offer. Besides being innocent and not having done anything to deserve the way they were treated, the inner child also has play, tenderness, irreverence, creativity, etc. to offer. And keep in mind that regardless of all that, the inner child is still worthy of love.

What to do if you cannot be your own parent yet

Thirdly, it often happens that people either can’t conjure up one of the above functions of the adult, or feel blank when they try, or only experience the ‘inherited internal critic’. Sometimes the problem is that the ‘adult’ doesn’t really feel like an adult, but instead feels like a child that is pretending to be an adult.

To solve this problem I use a technique that as far as I know, I developed (or at least combined in this way). I have no idea if it has been tried with people in therapy and if it works when all the parts are combined, but I find that it works for me.

Bring the Adult in by witnessing if that is necessary. If you can already differentiate the different ‘positions’ easily, skip this step and bring in the Adult that you need for this situation.

Borrow one of the Adult functions from someone else. Find a person in your life, a mentor, an older brother/sister, your own future self, a spiritual being, a value etc. that you think can be an Adult to you. Ask yourself what that person would say or do in the situation where you need that particular function (warmth, setting boundaries, knowing what’s best etc.) Be sure to only borrow what you need.

Now you become an apprentice of the Adult. Figure out yourself how you can say/do what you need in the situation. Make sure you at least do some of it yourself.

Now give the Adult functions back to the ‘borrowed’ person by telling them what they did and what 5% you can do now on your own.

It’s important not to let the ‘borrowed’ person take over your Adult functions, but to have them stand by you while you make the decision. For a more complete description of this, see my Inner Child Self Love Reparenting Guide .

Note: If you don’t have anyone in your life that you can remember that was a decent caretaker, then imagine someone who was, and make sure when you imagine what they would do, that you take into account your history. If you cannot even imagine being taken care of properly, start with ‘what the least cruel thing they could say/do?’ and when that starts working, move on to something better. Don’t keep doing variations of this exercise. Once you find something that works, try it out.

Also, you can use this technique when you feel that the ‘Adult’ doesn’t really feel like an adult. Ask yourself what a decent adult would do when the inner child says he/she doesn’t trust you. Don’t retaliate, don’t defend yourself by saying how good you are, don’t collapse and don’t leave. Just borrow one thing that a decent adult would do, even if you don’t feel old enough yet. You’ll get old later.

Let the Child speak without taking over Adult functions

While the above is happening, you may allow the ‘younger’ feeling state to come out and speak, but don’t give your Adult judgement functions to an outside ‘caretaker’ and don’t make yourself younger.

A good way to do this is to say something like: ‘You are allowed to speak, but know that my Adult is still here and will evaluate the situation and take care of you and will stop you if need be. I am not going into a younger state, neither am I going to listen to a guide, a recording or anyone else but my own Adult.’

This way you can get in touch with your wonder, playfulness, spontaneity, sensory perceptions, ability to express your needs and ability to quickly go from one emotion to the next, without also bringing in being obedient, helpless, scolding yourself and losing your Adult judgement.

Finally, even if the younger state doesn’t trust your love for him/her yet, that doesn’t mean that you can’t still love him/her.

Okay. I know that you don't believe me. And that's okay. I know that I still love you. And I know that you don't have to love me. But just tell me if there's something that you feel is not safe for you in what I'm doing, okay?

But that's not how we end a complaint. Be serious. When they hear our anger and don't retaliate, when we admit we really fucked up, when we repair with the position that attacked us internally, just like when we show up to make meals, set boundaries, go to appointments, and keep promises, all of this is part of the pattern of evidence to back up our words. It might feel like not retaliating when they're angry is a way of showing our love, but it doesn't replace having love; it doesn't make our love any less cold.

When they make a vow and then blame us for not believing them, notice if the one who's blaming and the one who's making the vow are a younger or older version of the same position, or if they're a blended position. Don't assume based on their chronological age.

Notice what it is they're trying to teach you. If you're in the position of the one being blamed, remember that you're in the position of a younger version of yourself. You didn't know what you know now. You made the best choice you could in that moment that you were willing to be aware of, with the consequences that resulted. Just because you did something harmful to someone (even if it's yourself) doesn't mean that punishing yourself helps. You still may need to take responsibility and make repairs, but punishing yourself isn't helpful.

The Two-Hand Practice

Place your hand over your chest (at your heart center) to connect with your ability to love physically. Place your other hand below your chest at your solar plexus to relate to the vulnerable child.

Send love from your heart to your child. See what you get back. It might take a few rounds for you to have a conversation.

Remember: The love is on top. The child is on the bottom. And you're in the middle.

The Nurturer

Your role as the nurturer is to offer your love and enjoy their company. It's as simple as that.

It's okay. I'm here. You don't have to do anything. You're not too much. You can be small. You can be angry. You can be sad. I'll be okay.

The Protector

Your job as the protector is to make the love feel real by protecting them.

I'll set that boundary. I won't engage in that unsafe conversation. I won't text that person. I'll make myself eat. I'll go to sleep. I'll keep that promise. I won't let you be responsible for adult stuff.

This is where a lot of people bullshit themselves when working with their inner child. As the adult, they may send destabilizing messages, fail to take care of themselves, not do what they need to do, and not keep promises. It starts to become real when you do the thing.

If you can't find the love, do the thing. It might be that you don't do the thing for the child, so figure out what's going on that's keeping you from doing the thing. It might not be that you're failing. It might just be that you were afraid, or tired, or didn't have the skills or didn't plan it out well, or whatever. Also, just because you didn't feel better right away doesn't mean that it didn't work. And just because you checked it off your list doesn't mean that it worked.

The Leader/Guide/Guru/Wise One/Sage/Inner Teacher/Director/Higher Adult

Your role in this triad is to give direction.

Sometimes that direction is hard. It's not always about being perfectly disciplined, but it's also okay for you to be the one to ask for help, to communicate what you want, to show your imperfections to safe people. It's okay to want to be close to people, but it's not okay to punish them when they need space. Figure out how to have it both ways.

You are here not just to feel good You are here to become whole You are here to be part of life You are here to serve truth, beauty and love You are here to serve God, source, nature, universe, dharma, Tao You are here to be of benefit to all beings

What will a healthy, mature adult do here? How can I get their help first?

Are protectors a useful way of putting it for you?

Most people assume that when I work with their inner child that I go straight to the child. That is rarely the case.

More often than not when I try and connect with their inner child… They go numb Or cynical Or angry Or hungry Or they feel the need to check their phone Or they feel a sexual urge Or they start planning their next day Or they go to sleep Or they dissociate Or they say “this is stupid” …

Another important voice is the inherited parent voice. This is the voice of the parent(s) the person has internalised as a child. It is different to my concept of the inner adult (Nurturer, Protector, Leader/Guru) which we work to create. Often this inherited parent voice is a critic or a warden. It tells the inner child not to cry, not to be needy, not to act in a way that would embarrass the parent, not to be independent, etc. This voice can often say “this isn’t real, this is fake, you’re just making this up” etc. when we try and bring in new, loving parent voices for the inner child.

What might this voice/feeling/urge be protecting me from? What might it be protecting my inner child from? How might I acknowledge this part and ask for it’s cooperation?

What might it be afraid would happen if it wasn’t here? If I wasn’t numb/cynical/angry/distracted? Would I be… Lying to myself Engaging in fantasy Engaging in a role Allowing myself to feel a pain that would destroy me Being spiritual instead of real Forgiving too soon Hearing a voice in my head that isn’t real Abandoning myself/my child at the end of the therapy session …

What can I do to gain this protector’s trust? Increase my trust by 1%?

What does this protector need from me? Usually it just needs me to do something simple: Keep a boundary Do a task Eat a meal Not send a text/message Keep a promise Go to sleep Make contact with my therapist Acknowledge a debt Write something down …

How might I protect myself in a more healthy, effective way?

The Protector isn’t just a voice in your head. It is also a way of moving through your body: Orient yourself Assess the situation Distinguish between real danger, uncertainty, and imagined danger Do one thing to protect yourself in proportion to the danger Assess if you are safe now Stand down from protection and let yourself rest …

The Protector is also a way of thinking: Acknowledge what you don’t know Ask other humans for help Refrain from interpreting things until you have more information Engage in “no trance” practice …

How might I reparent my inner child in this moment?

Reparenting therapy and self hypnosis are a perfect match. Sometimes the inner child will come forward as an age, an image, a body position, a voice, a memory, an emotion, or a sense of vulnerability. Often they won’t. That’s OK. Work with whatever you can identify: a protector, a sensation, a feeling, a preference, etc.

What to do once you see the child (TL;DR: Be with them for now, don’t try to heal them. Do this:

“ Hey, kiddo. It’s okay. I’m here. No need to talk. It’s okay that you’re like this. I’m not gonna try to heal you right now. You don’t need to impress me. What do you need? ”

Maybe they want to play, feel warm, be protected, grieve, be mad, eat, rest, push you away, be kept away from someone, stop fantasising, stop working too hard, or simply hear you promise that you will do something as an adult today for them.

Don’t rush to fix them. Take your time to:

1. Prepare yourself

2. Inspect the problem

3. Ask them what they need (warmth, contact, talking, space, nothing…)

4. Give them what they need (only one thing at a time)

5. Wait

6. Try to reconnect (don’t force the child to become a part of you, be a part of you, disappear, ‘forgive’ you, be happy…)

7. Rest

8. Evaluate the situation again later.

Remember, you don’t need to fix them completely and make them ‘good as new’, but ‘good as you’. If the term ‘parts’/’child parts’ is confusing to you, think of them as signals, feelings, younger versions of you, or whatever works.

Remember that even playing and resting require the ‘adult’ to be present - you’re not actually a child again, you don’t need to lose reality-testing in ‘re-parenting’. You’re not a child, pet, object or a doll that someone else owns, you’re you and you’re just trying to feel the emotions you missed out on. Play with a plushie, talk to it, draw, touch interesting things, do whatever seems interesting to the younger version of you.

When resting, remind yourself you don’t need to be completely helpless, but you can give yourself a break from making decisions for a set amount of time. You can also remind yourself that you can do the things you were supposed to do later, write them down so the ‘adult’ can see them later, while the ‘child’ rests. The ‘adult’ can also keep an eye out while the ‘child’ rests.

If you can’t talk to your ‘child’ or imagine a conversation, write it down, preferably using your non-dominant hand as the ‘child’ (or the protector you’re communicating with) and your dominant hand as the ‘adult’. It may feel weird and your handwriting will be bad, but it can work. E.g.

N-d h: I don’t trust you.

D h: That’s okay. I still love you. What did I do that made you feel that way? I won’t make you trust me, I’ll just hear you out and then promise to do something.

N-d h: What?

D h: Eat, clean my desk, not text that person…
